reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: The nasal bones are the most commonly fractured facial bones, and the diagnosis is largely clinical, based on deformity, swelling, epistaxis, tenderness, and mobility or crepitus of the nasal bridge
Plain radiographs add little to management, so imaging is reserved for suspicion of associated injuries such as naso-orbito-ethmoid or midface fractures
The nose should be examined internally with a speculum to exclude a septal haematoma, which is the key finding not to miss
A septal haematoma requires prompt drainage because untreated it can cause septal cartilage necrosis, perforation, and a saddle-nose deformity
It is important to establish the pre-injury shape of the nose, often with a photograph, to judge post-traumatic deformity accurately

Reduction, when needed, is best performed either within the first few hours before swelling develops or after several days once swelling subsides but before the fracture sets, generally within about two weeks
Persistent deformity or nasal obstruction after healing may need later formal septorhinoplasty rather than early manipulation
Clear rhinorrhoea after nasal trauma should raise concern for a CSF leak from an associated skull base or cribriform injury
reference.pathophysiology: The prominent, relatively thin nasal bones and the cartilaginous septum are readily displaced by frontal or lateral trauma. Lateral forces tend to displace the nasal bones to one side, while frontal impact can flatten and splay the bones and buckle the septum. Bleeding into the subperichondrial space of the septum forms a septal haematoma, which strips the perichondrium from the cartilage and deprives it of its blood supply; the resulting ischaemia and any superimposed infection can destroy the cartilage, leading to septal perforation and loss of dorsal support (saddle deformity). Higher-energy injuries may extend into the naso-orbito-ethmoid region or the skull base.
additionalDifferentials: Septal haematoma or septal fracture without nasal bone fracture
Nasal soft tissue contusion without fracture
Associated midface (Le Fort) or orbital fracture
Pre-existing nasal deformity mistaken for acute injury
Frontal sinus or skull base fracture with CSF leak
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination for external deformity, mobility, and airflow
Internal nasal examination with a speculum to exclude septal haematoma
Pre-injury photographs to assess the original nasal shape
CT when naso-orbito-ethmoid, midface, or skull base injury is suspected
Assessment for CSF rhinorrhoea if clear nasal discharge follows the injury
redFlags: Septal haematoma requiring urgent drainage to prevent cartilage necrosis
Clear rhinorrhoea suggesting a CSF leak from skull base or cribriform injury
Telecanthus, medial canthal disruption, or features of a naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture
Uncontrolled epistaxis or signs of a more extensive midface fracture
reference.prognosis: Most isolated nasal fractures heal well, and timely closed reduction gives good cosmetic and functional results in many patients. A proportion are left with residual deformity or nasal obstruction that may require later septorhinoplasty. The main preventable adverse outcome is the saddle-nose deformity and septal perforation that follow an undrained septal haematoma.
pitfalls: Failing to examine the septum and missing a septal haematoma
Relying on plain radiographs, which rarely change management
Attempting reduction during peak swelling, giving an inaccurate result
Delaying reduction beyond the window in which the fracture can be manipulated
Overlooking an associated naso-orbito-ethmoid or skull base injury
Not documenting the pre-injury appearance, leading to unrealistic expectations
management: Exclude and urgently drain a septal haematoma, the key finding not to miss, to prevent cartilage necrosis and saddle-nose deformity
Provide initial care with control of epistaxis, analgesia and reduction of swelling, and establish the pre-injury nasal shape with a photograph

Perform closed reduction of displaced fractures within the appropriate window, either before swelling develops or after it subsides but before the fracture sets, reserving open reduction or septorhinoplasty for complex or late deformity
Reserve CT imaging for suspected associated naso-orbito-ethmoid, midface or skull-base injury, and assess for CSF rhinorrhoea if clear discharge follows
Manage isolated fractures without routine radiographs, since the diagnosis is clinical
Consider antibiotic cover after septal haematoma drainage or when there is an associated open injury
Arrange ENT or plastic surgery follow-up to assess residual deformity or nasal obstruction, with later septorhinoplasty if needed
